statement: Let $R$ be a [semiprime ring](c:semiprime-ring) with finite uniform dimension as a right module over itself and the [ascending chain condition](c:ascending-chain-condition) on right [annihilators](c:annihilator). Then the regular elements of $R$ satisfy the right [Ore condition](c:ore-condition), and the right classical ring of quotients of $R$ is a [semisimple ring](c:semisimple-ring) that is [Artinian](c:artinian-ring).

hypotheses.text: The ring $R$ is [semiprime](c:semiprime-ring): it has no nonzero nilpotent ideal.
The right module $R_R$ has finite uniform dimension: it holds no infinite direct sum of nonzero right ideals.
The ring $R$ has the [ascending chain condition](c:ascending-chain-condition) on right [annihilators](c:annihilator) of subsets of $R$.

conclusion: The regular elements of $R$ form a right Ore set, and the localization $Q$ at them is a semisimple Artinian ring.

proofs.name: Essential right ideals hold regular elements
proofs.slogan: Show that essential right ideals contain regular elements, deduce the Ore condition, and show that the quotient ring is semisimple.
proofs.scope: The forward direction of Goldie's theorem, as an outline of the cited proof. The converse (a ring with a semisimple Artinian right classical quotient ring is semiprime right Goldie) is the other half and is not proved here.

roles.why: Semiprimeness turns a nilpotent ideal into the zero ideal, so the singular ideal vanishes.
Finite uniform dimension makes $aR$ essential once $a$ has zero right annihilator, and bounds the length of $Q$.
The chain condition makes the singular ideal nilpotent and lets one choose an element with zero right annihilator.

steps.slogan: Show that the right singular ideal of $R$ is zero.
steps.detail: With the [ascending chain condition](c:ascending-chain-condition) on right annihilators, the right singular ideal is nilpotent. A [semiprime ring](c:semiprime-ring) has no nonzero nilpotent ideal, so no nonzero element has an essential right annihilator.

steps.slogan: Find a regular element inside every essential right ideal.
steps.detail: Finite uniform dimension and the chain condition on [annihilators](c:annihilator) give an element $a$ of the [essential](c:essential-ideal) right ideal with right annihilator zero. Then $aR \cong R_R$ is essential, and $xa = 0$ gives $x$ an essential right annihilator, so $x = 0$ by step 1 and $a$ is regular. A right ideal that holds a regular element is essential by the same argument.

steps.slogan: Derive the right [Ore condition](c:ore-condition) for the regular elements.
steps.detail: Let $a$ be regular and $b \in R$. The right ideal $\{r : br \in aR\}$ is essential because $aR$ is, so it holds a regular element $c$ by step 2. Then $bc = ad$ for some $d$, which is the right Ore condition, and Ore's construction gives the right classical ring of quotients $Q$.

steps.slogan: Show that every right ideal of $Q$ is a direct summand, so $Q$ is semisimple Artinian.
steps.detail: Let $J$ be a right ideal of $Q$ and $J'$ a complement, so $J \oplus J'$ is essential in $Q$. Its trace on $R$ is essential in $R$, so it holds a regular element of $R$, which is a unit of $Q$, hence $J \oplus J' = Q$. Thus $Q$ is a [semisimple ring](c:semisimple-ring) of finite length, hence [Artinian](c:artinian-ring), and the Artin-Wedderburn theorem splits it into matrix rings over division rings.

concepts.c:semiprime-ring: Semiprimeness removes nilpotent ideals, which makes the singular ideal zero.
concepts.c:ascending-chain-condition: The chain condition on annihilators controls the singular ideal and the choice of element.
concepts.c:annihilator: Right annihilators decide when an element is regular or singular.
concepts.c:essential-ideal: Essential right ideals are the ones that must contain regular elements.
concepts.c:ore-condition: The Ore condition lets one form fractions with regular denominators.
concepts.c:semisimple-ring: The quotient ring splits as a direct sum of simple right ideals.
concepts.c:artinian-ring: Finite uniform dimension makes the semisimple quotient ring Artinian.

source.ref: A. W. Goldie, Semi-prime rings with maximum condition, Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society (3) 10 (1960), 201-220
source.note: The four steps list the ingredients of Goldie's proof in order; T. Y. Lam, Lectures on Modules and Rings (Springer, 1999) gives a textbook account.

statement: For finitely generated groups $A$ and $B$, the [rank](c:rank-of-a-group) of the [free product](c:free-product) $A * B$ equals $\operatorname{rank}(A) + \operatorname{rank}(B)$.

hypotheses.text: The groups $A$ and $B$ have finite [generating sets](c:generating-set).

proofs.name: Stallings folding
proofs.slogan: Split any generating map from a free group along the free product by folding graphs, then count ranks.
proofs.scope: Finite ranks; for an infinite rank $\operatorname{rank}(A*B) \ge \operatorname{rank} A$ holds because $A$ is a quotient of $A*B$, and the sum is cardinal addition. The steps outline Stallings' proof of the splitting form of Grushko's theorem.

roles.why: Finite generating sets give the upper bound and a free group $F_n$ of finite rank onto $A*B$.

steps.slogan: Join generating sets of $A$ and $B$ to bound the rank of $A * B$ from above.
steps.detail: The union of a [generating set](c:generating-set) of $A$ and one of $B$ generates $A * B$. So $\operatorname{rank}(A*B) \le \operatorname{rank} A + \operatorname{rank} B$, and the reverse inequality remains.

steps.slogan: Take a [surjection](c:surjection) $\varphi$ from a [free group](c:free-group) of minimal rank $n$ onto $A * B$.
steps.detail: Let $n = \operatorname{rank}(A*B)$ and send a free basis of $F_n$ to a generating set of $A * B$. The aim is to split $F_n$ along $\varphi$.

steps.slogan: Realize $\varphi$ by a map of graphs and simplify the map by Stallings folds.
steps.detail: Stallings realizes $F_n$ as the fundamental group of a graph and $\varphi$ as a map into a space built from a $K(A,1)$ and a $K(B,1)$ joined by an edge, transverse to the midpoint of that edge. Folding edges with equal images keeps the map onto on fundamental groups, and the rank stays $n$ because it cannot fall below $n$.

steps.slogan: Read a free splitting $F_n = F' * F''$ from the reduced graph.
steps.detail: In the reduced graph the preimage of the midpoint cuts the graph into pieces that map into the $A$-side or the $B$-side. The fundamental group is then a free product of a part $F'$ with $\varphi(F') \le A$ and a part $F''$ with $\varphi(F'') \le B$.

steps.slogan: Add the ranks of the two factors to match the upper bound.
steps.detail: Since $\varphi$ is onto, $\varphi(F') = A$ and $\varphi(F'') = B$: subgroups $A' \le A$ and $B' \le B$ generate $A' * B'$, which equals $A * B$ only when $A' = A$ and $B' = B$. So $n = \operatorname{rank} F' + \operatorname{rank} F'' \ge \operatorname{rank} A + \operatorname{rank} B$, and with step 1 the ranks add.

concepts.c:rank-of-a-group: The rank is the quantity that the theorem computes for the free product.
concepts.c:free-product: The splitting of the free group must match the free product decomposition.
concepts.c:generating-set: Generating sets of the factors give the upper bound for the rank.
concepts.c:surjection: Surjectivity of $\varphi$ forces the images of the two parts to be all of $A$ and $B$.
concepts.c:free-group: Free groups have additive rank, which turns the splitting into a count.

source.ref: J. R. Stallings, A topological proof of Grushko's theorem on free products, Mathematische Zeitschrift 90 (1965), 1-8
source.note: The steps list the ingredients of Stallings' folding proof of the statement that every epimorphism from a free group onto $A*B$ splits; Grushko (1940) and Neumann (1943) proved the rank formula first.

statement: If $G$ is a [perfect group](c:is-perfect), then the [center](c:center) of the [quotient group](c:quotient-group) $G/Z(G)$ is trivial.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is [perfect](c:is-perfect): its commutator subgroup is $G$.

proofs.name: Second center and three subgroups
proofs.slogan: Show that the second center of a perfect group equals the center, using the Three Subgroups Lemma.
proofs.scope: The whole lemma, for every perfect group $G$ including the trivial group.

roles.why: Perfectness replaces the commutator subgroup $[G,G]$ by $G$, which turns a double commutator into $[G, Z_2]$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite the claim as an inclusion of the second center in the center.
steps.detail: Let $Z_2$ be the preimage of $Z(G/Z(G))$ in $G$. It is the second term of the [upper central series](c:upper-central-series), and $Z(G/Z(G))$ is trivial exactly when $Z_2 \le Z(G)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the commutator of $Z_2$ with $G$ lies in the center.
steps.detail: For $z \in Z_2$ and $g \in G$, the class of $[z,g]$ in $G/Z(G)$ is the commutator of a central element with $gZ(G)$, so it is trivial. Hence $[Z_2, G] \le Z(G)$, and the double commutators $[[Z_2,G],G]$ and $[[G,Z_2],G]$ are trivial.

steps.slogan: Combine the two trivial double commutators by the Three Subgroups Lemma.
steps.detail: The lemma, which rests on the Hall-Witt identity, says that if two of $[[A,B],C]$, $[[B,C],A]$, $[[C,A],B]$ are trivial then so is the third. With $A = Z_2$ and $B = C = G$ it gives $[[G,G],Z_2] = 1$.

steps.slogan: Replace $[G,G]$ by $G$ because $G$ is perfect.
steps.detail: Since $G$ is [perfect](c:is-perfect), its [commutator subgroup](c:commutator-subgroup) is $G$, so $[[G,G],Z_2] = [G, Z_2] = 1$. Thus every element of $Z_2$ commutes with all of $G$, that is $Z_2 \le Z(G)$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the center of $G/Z(G)$ is trivial.
steps.detail: Since $Z(G) \le Z_2 \le Z(G)$, the preimage of $Z(G/Z(G))$ is exactly $Z(G)$. So $Z(G/Z(G))$ is the trivial subgroup.

concepts.c:is-perfect: Perfectness is the hypothesis that makes $[G,G] = G$.
concepts.c:center: The claim is that the center of the quotient is trivial.
concepts.c:quotient-group: The quotient $G/Z(G)$ is the group whose center is computed.
concepts.c:upper-central-series: The preimage of the center of the quotient is the second term of this series.
concepts.c:commutator-subgroup: Perfectness says the commutator subgroup is the whole group.

source.note: mathlib moves the claim to the second center (Subgroup.comap_upperCentralSeries_quotient_center), then proves Z_2(G) = Z(G) for perfect G (Group.IsPerfect.upperCentralSeries_eq_center) with Subgroup.commutator_commutator_eq_bot_of_rotate, the Three Subgroups Lemma.

statement: Let $M$ be a linearly [ordered module](c:is-ordered-module) over an Archimedean ordered division ring $K$, and $R$ an Archimedean ordered $K$-module for which a seed exists. Then a strictly monotone $K$-linear map $f$ from $M$ into the lexicographically ordered [Hahn series](c:hahn-series) $R[[\Gamma]]$ over the [Archimedean classes](c:archimedean-class) $\Gamma$ of $M$ exists, and the leading exponent of $f(a)$ is the class of $a$.

hypotheses.text: $K$ is a division ring with a linear order that makes it an Archimedean ordered ring.
$M$ is a linearly [ordered module](c:is-ordered-module) over $K$: an ordered abelian group with an ordered $K$-action.
$R$ is an [Archimedean](c:archimedean) ordered abelian group with a $K$-module structure.
A seed exists: complements of the open Archimedean ball in the closed ball of each class of $M$, with strictly monotone $K$-linear coefficient maps from these strata to $R$.

conclusion: There is a strictly monotone $K$-linear map $f\colon M \to R[[\Gamma]]$ (lexicographic order) such that the leading exponent of $f(a)$ is the Archimedean class of $a$, for every $a \in M$.

proofs.name: Maximal partial embedding
proofs.slogan: Extend partial Hahn embeddings one element at a time and take a maximal one by Zorn's lemma.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, including the zero element and a module with finitely many Archimedean classes. With $K = \mathbb{Q}$ and $R = \mathbb{R}$ a seed always exists, which gives the classical Hahn embedding theorem.

roles.why: The Archimedean property of $K$ makes the balls submodules and the strata Archimedean.
The order and the $K$-action on $M$ make Archimedean classes and strictly monotone linear maps meaningful.
The [Archimedean](c:archimedean) property of $R$ lets the extension keep leading exponents equal to classes.
The seed supplies the base embedding, which makes the family of partial embeddings nonempty.

steps.slogan: Build the base embedding from the seed on the sum of the strata.
steps.detail: Each Archimedean class $c$ has a stratum, a complement of the open ball in the closed ball of $c$. The strata are independent, so their sum has a base embedding into $R[[\Gamma]]$ that places the seed's coefficient map at position $c$.

steps.slogan: Define partial Hahn embeddings as strictly monotone, truncation-closed extensions of the base embedding.
steps.detail: A partial Hahn embedding is a $K$-linear map on a submodule of $M$ that extends the base embedding, is strictly monotone, and has every truncation of a value in its range. It sends the class of $x$ to the leading exponent of its value.

steps.slogan: Extend each partial embedding properly by one element outside its domain.
steps.detail: For $x$ outside the domain, take each coefficient of the new value from a domain element whose difference with $x$ lies in a higher class, and set the value at $x$ to the resulting series. The map on the domain plus $Kx$ is again strictly monotone and truncation-closed, and strictly larger; this uses that $R$ is Archimedean.

steps.slogan: Take a maximal partial embedding by Zorn's lemma.
steps.detail: Order the partial embeddings by extension. The union of a chain is a partial embedding, since the defining properties concern single elements, so every chain has an upper bound. Zorn's lemma gives a maximal element, and the set is nonempty because the base embedding belongs to it.

steps.slogan: Show that the maximal embedding has domain $M$ and read off the conclusion.
steps.detail: If some $x$ lay outside the domain, step 3 would give a strictly larger partial embedding, against maximality. So the domain is $M$, and the map is strictly monotone and $K$-linear with leading exponent of $f(a)$ equal to the class of $a$.

concepts.c:is-ordered-module: An ordered module is the kind of structure that the embedding must respect.
concepts.c:hahn-series: Hahn series with lexicographic order form the target of the embedding.
concepts.c:archimedean-class: Archimedean classes index the exponents of the Hahn series.
concepts.c:archimedean: Archimedean behaviour of $R$ makes leading exponents record classes exactly.

source.note: mathlib builds Seed.baseEmbedding, extends one element at a time (HahnEmbedding.Partial.extend, lt_extend), takes a maximal partial embedding with zorn_le_nonempty (exists_isMax) and shows its domain is all of M (exists_domain_eq_top).

statement: Let $M$ be a [closed oriented manifold](c:closed-oriented-manifold) of dimension 4 that carries an [Einstein metric](c:einstein-metric). Then its [Euler characteristic](c:euler-characteristic) $\chi(M)$ and its [signature](c:signature) $\tau(M)$ satisfy $\chi(M) \ge \tfrac{3}{2}\,|\tau(M)|$.

hypotheses.text: $M$ is a [closed oriented manifold](c:closed-oriented-manifold) of dimension 4: smooth, compact, without boundary.
$M$ has a Riemannian metric $g$ with $\mathrm{Ric}(g) = \lambda g$ for a constant $\lambda$, an [Einstein metric](c:einstein-metric).

proofs.name: Curvature integrals
proofs.slogan: Write the Euler characteristic and the signature as curvature integrals, then compare them for a metric with zero trace-free Ricci tensor.
proofs.scope: Every closed oriented Einstein 4-manifold, with norms taken on 2-forms so that the constants below are correct. Equality cases such as the K3 surface are not analysed.

roles.why: Closedness and orientation make the two curvature integrals compute topological invariants.
The Einstein condition makes the trace-free Ricci tensor vanish.

steps.slogan: Write the [Euler characteristic](c:euler-characteristic) as an integral of curvature terms.
steps.detail: The Gauss-Bonnet-Chern formula in dimension 4 gives $\chi(M) = \frac{1}{8\pi^2}\int_M \big(|W^+|^2 + |W^-|^2 + \tfrac{s^2}{24} - \tfrac12 |\mathring{\mathrm{Ric}}|^2\big)\,dv$. Here $W^\pm$ are the self-dual and anti-self-dual parts of the [Weyl tensor](c:weyl-tensor), $s$ is the scalar curvature and $\mathring{\mathrm{Ric}}$ is the trace-free [Ricci tensor](c:ricci-curvature).

steps.slogan: Write the [signature](c:signature) as an integral of $|W^+|^2 - |W^-|^2$.
steps.detail: The Hirzebruch signature theorem gives $\tau(M) = \tfrac13 \langle p_1(M), [M] \rangle$. Chern-Weil theory writes $p_1$ through curvature, which gives $\tau(M) = \frac{1}{12\pi^2}\int_M \big(|W^+|^2 - |W^-|^2\big)\,dv$.

steps.slogan: Remove the trace-free Ricci term by the Einstein condition.
steps.detail: For $\mathrm{Ric} = \lambda g$ the trace-free part $\mathring{\mathrm{Ric}}$ is zero. The integrand of step 1 reduces to $|W^+|^2 + |W^-|^2 + s^2/24$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two formulas into integrals for $2\chi \mp 3\tau$.
steps.detail: Multiply the formula for $\chi$ by 2 and the formula for $\tau$ by 3, then subtract or add. This gives $2\chi(M) \mp 3\tau(M) = \frac{1}{4\pi^2}\int_M \big(2|W^\mp|^2 + \tfrac{s^2}{24}\big)\,dv$.

steps.slogan: Read the sign of each integrand to get $2\chi \ge 3|\tau|$.
steps.detail: Both integrands are nonnegative, so $2\chi - 3\tau \ge 0$ and $2\chi + 3\tau \ge 0$. Hence $2\chi(M) \ge 3|\tau(M)|$.

concepts.c:closed-oriented-manifold: Closed and oriented are needed for the integrals and the index theorems.
concepts.c:einstein-metric: The Einstein metric has no trace-free Ricci part, which removes the negative term.
concepts.c:euler-characteristic: The Euler characteristic is one side of the inequality.
concepts.c:signature: The signature is the other side of the inequality.
concepts.c:weyl-tensor: Its self-dual and anti-self-dual parts carry the integrand of the signature.
concepts.c:ricci-curvature: The trace-free Ricci tensor is the only term with a negative sign.

source.note: The argument of Hitchin, On compact four-dimensional Einstein manifolds, J. Differential Geom. 9 (1974), 435-441, after Thorpe; the curvature formulas are in Besse, Einstein Manifolds (Springer, 1987).

statement: Let $(X,g)$ be a closed oriented [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) of dimension $n$ with [Hodge star](c:hodge-star) $\star$. For each exact $(n-k+1)$-form $j$, every class of degree $k$ in [de Rham cohomology](c:de-rham-cohomology) holds exactly one closed $k$-form $F$ with $d\star F = j$. For $j = 0$ this $F$ is the [harmonic form](c:harmonic-form) of the class.

hypotheses.text: $(X,g)$ is a closed oriented [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) of dimension $n$.
$c$ is a class of degree $k$ in [de Rham cohomology](c:de-rham-cohomology).
$j$ is an exact $(n-k+1)$-form on $X$.

conclusion: Exactly one closed $k$-form $F$ in the class $c$ satisfies $d\star F = j$.

proofs.name: Hodge decomposition and Green operator
proofs.slogan: Start from the harmonic representative, solve for the exact correction with the Green operator, and prove uniqueness by integration by parts.
proofs.scope: The whole statement with a source $j$. For $k = 2$ and $n = 4$, $F$ is the Faraday 2-form and $j$ the current, and $j = 0$ is the vacuum case, the Hodge theorem itself.

roles.why: Compactness gives the Hodge theorem and the Green operator, and closedness makes integration by parts free of boundary terms.
The class $c$ supplies the harmonic representative that the solution starts from.
Exactness of $j$ makes $\star j$ orthogonal to harmonic forms, which makes the equation solvable.

steps.slogan: Split the class into its harmonic representative plus an exact form.
steps.detail: The Hodge theorem gives a [harmonic form](c:harmonic-form) $F_h$ in the class $c$. Harmonic forms on a closed manifold are closed and coclosed, so $d\star F_h = 0$, and every closed form in $c$ is $F_h + d\alpha$ with $\alpha$ a $(k-1)$-form.

steps.slogan: Reduce the source equation to an equation for $\alpha$ alone.
steps.detail: Because $d\star F_h = 0$, we get $d\star(F_h + d\alpha) = d\star d\alpha$. With the codifferential $\delta = \pm\star d\star$, the equation $d\star d\alpha = j$ becomes $\delta d\alpha = \pm\omega$ for the $(k-1)$-form $\omega = \star j$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\omega$ is coclosed and orthogonal to the harmonic $(k-1)$-forms.
steps.detail: Since $j$ is exact, $dj = 0$, so $\delta\omega = \pm\star dj = 0$. For a harmonic form $h$ and $j = d\beta$, $\langle\omega, h\rangle = \pm\int_X h \wedge d\beta = \pm\int_X d(h \wedge \beta) = 0$ by Stokes' theorem, because $dh = 0$ and $X$ is closed.

steps.slogan: Solve $\delta d\alpha = \pm\omega$ with the Green operator of the Laplacian.
steps.detail: The Green operator $G$ of the Hodge Laplacian $\Delta$ satisfies $\Delta G\omega = \omega - H\omega$ with $H$ the harmonic projection, and $G$ commutes with $\delta$. Here $H\omega = 0$ and $\delta\omega = 0$, so $\alpha = \pm G\omega$ gives $\delta d\alpha = \Delta\alpha - d\delta\alpha = \pm\omega$.

steps.slogan: Show that two solutions are equal by an integration by parts.
steps.detail: Two closed forms in the class $c$ with the same $d\star F$ differ by an exact form $d\eta$ with $d\star d\eta = 0$. Then $\|d\eta\|^2 = \langle \eta, \delta d\eta \rangle = 0$ because $\delta d\eta = \pm\star d\star d\eta = 0$, so $d\eta = 0$.

steps.slogan: Combine the solution $F_h + d\alpha$ with uniqueness to get exactly one form.
steps.detail: The form $F = F_h + d\alpha$ lies in $c$, is closed and satisfies $d\star F = j$. By step 5 it is the only such form. For $j = 0$ we may take $\alpha = 0$, so $F = F_h$ is the harmonic representative.

concepts.c:riemannian-manifold: The metric gives the Hodge star, the codifferential and the Laplacian.
concepts.c:de-rham-cohomology: The class $c$ is the datum whose representatives the theorem counts.
concepts.c:harmonic-form: The harmonic representative is the starting point and the solution for $j = 0$.
concepts.c:hodge-star: The star turns the source $j$ into the form $\omega$ and defines the codifferential.

source.note: Hodge theory (harmonic representatives, Green operator) as in Warner, Foundations of Differentiable Manifolds and Lie Groups, chapter 6; the source term follows from the Hodge decomposition.

statement: Let $P$ be a polynomial in $y_0, \dots, y_n$ whose coefficients are rational functions of $z$. If $P(z; \Gamma(z), \Gamma'(z), \dots, \Gamma^{(n)}(z)) = 0$ for all $z$, where $\Gamma$ is the [gamma function](c:gamma-function), then $P = 0$.

hypotheses.text: $\Gamma$ is the [gamma function](c:gamma-function): [meromorphic](c:meromorphic-function) on $\mathbb{C}$, without zeros, with $\Gamma(z+1) = z\,\Gamma(z)$.
$P \in \mathbb{C}(z)[y_0, \dots, y_n]$ satisfies $P(z; \Gamma, \Gamma', \dots, \Gamma^{(n)}) \equiv 0$.

conclusion: $P$ is the zero polynomial, so $\Gamma$ satisfies no algebraic differential equation over $\mathbb{C}(z)$ and is transcendental in the sense of [differential algebra](c:differential-algebra).

proofs.name: Shift invariance for the digamma function
proofs.slogan: Pass to the digamma function, shift its argument by one, and show that a shift-compatible relation among derivatives is impossible.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for coefficients in $K = \mathbb{C}(z)$; polynomial coefficients are a special case. The proof shows that the [digamma function](c:digamma-function) $\psi = \Gamma'/\Gamma$ satisfies no such equation.

roles.why: The functional equation of $\Gamma$ gives $\psi(z+1) = \psi(z) + 1/z$, and the absence of zeros makes $\psi$ meromorphic.
The equation puts $\Gamma$ in a field of finite transcendence degree over $K$, which carries over to $\psi$.

steps.slogan: Pass from $\Gamma$ to its logarithmic derivative $\psi$.
steps.detail: A [meromorphic](c:meromorphic-function) function $f$ satisfies an algebraic differential equation over $K = \mathbb{C}(z)$ exactly when $K(f, f', f'', \dots)$ has [finite transcendence degree](c:fin-trdeg). That field is closed under $d/dz$, so an equation for $\Gamma$ gives one for $\psi = \Gamma'/\Gamma$. Also $\psi(z+1) = \psi(z) + r(z)$ with $r = 1/z$, hence $\psi^{(i)}(z+1) = \psi^{(i)}(z) + r^{(i)}(z)$.

steps.slogan: Choose the least $n$ for which $\psi^{(n)}$ is algebraic over the lower derivatives.
steps.detail: Suppose $\psi$ satisfies an equation, and let $n$ be least such that $\psi^{(n)}$ is algebraic over $L = K(\psi, \dots, \psi^{(n-1)})$. Then $\psi, \dots, \psi^{(n-1)}$ are [algebraically independent](c:algebraically-independent-subset) over $K$. Let $M(Y) = Y^d + c_{d-1}Y^{d-1} + \dots + c_0$ with $c_j \in L$ be the [minimal polynomial](c:minimal-polynomial) of $\psi^{(n)}$ over $L$.

steps.slogan: Shift the argument by one and compare the second coefficients of the minimal polynomial.
steps.detail: The shift $\sigma f(z) = f(z+1)$ maps $L$ onto itself, since $\sigma\psi^{(i)} = \psi^{(i)} + r^{(i)}$, so $\sigma(M)$ is the minimal polynomial of $\psi^{(n)} + r^{(n)}$, that is $M(Y - r^{(n)})$. Comparing the coefficients of $Y^{d-1}$ gives $\sigma(u) = u + r^{(n)}$ for $u = -c_{d-1}/d \in L$. By independence $L \cong F_n = K(y_0, \dots, y_{n-1})$, and $\sigma$ becomes the automorphism $T$ with $Tz = z+1$ and $Ty_i = y_i + r^{(i)}$, so some $h \in F_n$ has $Th - h = r^{(n)}$.

steps.slogan: Prove the claim for $n = 0$ by comparing the poles of a rational function.
steps.detail: Claim($n$): if $h \in F_n$ and $Th - h = \sum_i c_i r^{(i)}$ with constants $c_i$, then $c_i = 0$ for $i \ge n$, and $Th = h$ forces $h$ constant. For $n = 0$ the right side has poles only at $0$; a pole of $h$ of largest real part would sit at $0$ and one of smallest real part at $1$, which is impossible, so $h$ is a polynomial and all $c_i = 0$. A rational $h$ with $h(z+1) = h(z)$ takes one value at infinitely many points, so it is constant.

steps.slogan: Show that $h$ is a polynomial in $y_{n-1}$ over $F_{n-1}$.
steps.detail: Write $F_n = F_{n-1}(y)$ with $Ty = y + a$, $a = r^{(n-1)}$, and $h = p + s/q$ with $p$ a polynomial in $y$, $q$ monic and $\deg_y s < \deg_y q$. As $Th - h$ has no $y$, the quotient $T(s/q) - s/q$ is a polynomial whose numerator has smaller degree than its denominator, so it is $0$ and $Tq = q$. The $y^{e-1}$ coefficient of $q$, with $e = \deg_y q$, then satisfies $T q_{e-1} - q_{e-1} = -e\,a$, which Claim($n-1$) forbids unless $e = 0$; so $h = p$.

steps.slogan: Compare the top two coefficients of $h$ in $y_{n-1}$ to finish the induction.
steps.detail: Let $h = \sum_{j \le m} p_j y^j$ with $p_m \ne 0$ and $m \ge 1$. The top coefficient is $T$-invariant, so $p_m = c$ is a constant by Claim($n-1$), and $Tp_{m-1} - p_{m-1} = -mc\,r^{(n-1)}$, plus the right side $\sum c_i r^{(i)}$ if $m = 1$. Claim($n-1$) rules this out for $m \ge 2$, gives $c_i = 0$ for $i \ge n$ if $m = 1$, and applies to $h$ directly if $m = 0$; the same count with right side $0$ shows that invariants are constant.

steps.slogan: Contradict Claim($n$) with the equation $Th - h = r^{(n)}$.
steps.detail: The equation has $c_n = 1$ and all other $c_i = 0$, but Claim($n$) gives $c_n = 0$. So $\psi$ satisfies no algebraic differential equation over $K$, and neither does $\Gamma$.

concepts.c:gamma-function: Its functional equation $\Gamma(z+1) = z\Gamma(z)$ drives the whole argument.
concepts.c:meromorphic-function: The shift acts on the field of meromorphic functions, and $\psi$ lives there.
concepts.c:differential-algebra: The theorem says that $\Gamma$ is not differentially algebraic over rational functions.
concepts.c:digamma-function: The digamma function has the additive shift rule $\psi(z+1) = \psi(z) + 1/z$.
concepts.c:fin-trdeg: An algebraic differential equation means finite transcendence degree of the derivative field.
concepts.c:algebraically-independent-subset: Independence turns the field $L$ into a field of rational functions in indeterminates.
concepts.c:minimal-polynomial: The second coefficient of the minimal polynomial yields the shift relation for $u$.

source.note: A shift-invariance argument for the digamma function in the spirit of the difference-algebra proofs of Hölder's theorem (O. Hölder, Mathematische Annalen 28 (1887), 1-13); it is not a transcription of one published proof.

statement: A typist presses keys on a keyboard with finitely many keys, each stroke [independent](c:independent-random-variables) of the others and hitting key $a$ with the same probability $p_a > 0$. Then with [probability](c:probability-measure) 1 every finite text occurs infinitely often in the sequence of strokes.

hypotheses.text: The keyboard has finitely many keys, and each stroke hits key $a$ with probability $p_a > 0$.
The strokes are [independent](c:independent-random-variables) and identically distributed.

conclusion: With probability 1, every finite text appears infinitely often among the strokes.

proofs.name: Second Borel-Cantelli lemma
proofs.slogan: Cut the strokes into blocks, note that block events are independent with equal positive probability, and apply the second Borel-Cantelli lemma to each text.
proofs.scope: A fixed finite text first, then all texts together. The empty text is trivial, and a keyboard with one key is covered since $p_a = 1$.

roles.why: Positive key probabilities make a block spell the text with positive probability, and finitely many keys make the set of texts countable.
Independence of strokes gives independent block events, and equal distribution gives equal block probabilities.

steps.slogan: Cut the stroke sequence into consecutive blocks as long as the text.
steps.detail: Fix a text $w = w_1 \dots w_m$. Let $E_k$ be the event that the strokes $km+1, \dots, km+m$ spell $w$, for $k = 0, 1, 2, \dots$.

steps.slogan: Show that the block events $E_k$ are [independent](c:independence).
steps.detail: Each $E_k$ depends only on the strokes of block $k$, and distinct blocks use disjoint sets of strokes. Functions of disjoint groups of independent strokes are independent, so $E_0, E_1, \dots$ are independent.

steps.slogan: Compute the common probability of the events and show that their sum diverges.
steps.detail: By independence of the strokes, $\Pr(E_k) = p_{w_1} \cdots p_{w_m} =: p > 0$ for every $k$. So $\sum_k \Pr(E_k) = \infty$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that infinitely many events $E_k$ occur with probability 1.
steps.detail: The events $E_k$ are independent and the sum of their probabilities is infinite. The second Borel-Cantelli lemma gives $\Pr(E_k \text{ infinitely often}) = 1$.

steps.slogan: Intersect the probability-one events over all finite texts.
steps.detail: The set of finite texts over a finite alphabet is countable, and a countable intersection of events of probability 1 has probability 1. So almost surely every finite text occurs infinitely often.

concepts.c:independent-random-variables: Independent strokes are what make the block events independent.
concepts.c:probability-measure: The conclusion is an event of probability 1.
concepts.c:independence: The second Borel-Cantelli lemma needs independent events.

source.note: The standard application of the second Borel-Cantelli lemma; see Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, the section on the Borel-Cantelli lemmas.

statement: Let $T$ be a [compact operator](c:compact-operator) on a complex [Banach space](c:banach-space) $X$ with $\dim X \ge 2$. Then $T$ has a closed [invariant subspace](c:invariant-subspace) $Y$ with $\{0\} \ne Y \ne X$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a complex [Banach space](c:banach-space) with $\dim X \ge 2$.
$T$ is a [compact operator](c:compact-operator) on $X$.

conclusion: There is a closed subspace $Y$ with $\{0\} \ne Y \ne X$ and $T(Y) \subseteq Y$.

proofs.name: Lomonosov's argument with Schauder's theorem
proofs.slogan: Assume that the commutant of $T$ is transitive, find a commuting compact operator with an eigenvector by a fixed point argument, and contradict transitivity.
proofs.scope: The Aronszajn-Smith case of compact operators; the proof gives a closed subspace invariant under every operator that commutes with $T$. The general invariant subspace problem for bounded operators is not treated here.

roles.why: Complex scalars give eigenvalues in finite dimension, and completeness gives Mazur's theorem and Schauder's theorem.
Compactness makes $K = \overline{T(B)}$ compact and makes the eigenspace of a nonzero eigenvalue finite dimensional.

steps.slogan: Reduce to a nonzero compact $T$ on an infinite-dimensional space with transitive commutant.
steps.detail:
If $\dim X < \infty$ an [eigenvector](c:eigenvector) spans a suitable line, and if $T = 0$ any line works. Otherwise let $\mathcal{A}$ be the algebra of bounded operators that commute with $T$. If $\overline{\mathcal{A}y} 
e X$ for some $y 
e 0$, that closed subspace is nonzero and invariant under $T$, so assume $\mathcal{A}y$ is [dense](c:dense-set) for every $y 
e 0$ and look for a contradiction.

steps.slogan: Choose a ball $B$ whose image under $T$ stays away from zero.
steps.detail: Scale $T$ so that $\|T\| = 1$, take a unit vector $u$ with $\|Tu\| > \tfrac12$ and put $x_0 = 3u$. For $B = \{x : \|x - x_0\| \le 1\}$ we get $0 \notin B$ and $\|Tx\| \ge \|Tx_0\| - 1 > 0$ on $B$, so the compact set $K = \overline{T(B)}$ does not contain $0$.

steps.slogan: Cover $K$ by finitely many open sets given by operators of the commutant.
steps.detail: For each $y \in K$ the set $\mathcal{A}y$ is dense, so some $S \in \mathcal{A}$ has $\|Sy - x_0\| < 1$. These conditions define open sets that cover $K$, so finitely many $S_1, \dots, S_r$ suffice. With $\psi_j(y) = \max(0, 1 - \|S_j y - x_0\|)$ the functions $\phi_j = \psi_j / \sum_i \psi_i$ form a partition of unity on $K$.

steps.slogan: Build the map $\Phi$ from $B$ to $B$ and find its fixed point $x_1$.
steps.detail: Put $\Phi(x) = \sum_j \phi_j(Tx)\, S_j T x$. Each value is a convex combination of points within distance 1 of $x_0$, so $\Phi$ is continuous from $B$ into $B$. Its image lies in the closed [convex hull](c:convex-hull) of the compact sets $\overline{S_j T(B)}$, which is compact by Mazur's theorem, so Schauder's theorem gives $x_1 \in B$ with $\Phi(x_1) = x_1$, and $x_1 \ne 0$.

steps.slogan: Turn the fixed point into an [eigenvector](c:eigenvector) of $T$.
steps.detail: Let $S = \sum_j \phi_j(Tx_1) S_j \in \mathcal{A}$, so $STx_1 = x_1$. The operator $ST$ is compact and commutes with $T$, so $N = \ker(ST - I)$ is a nonzero finite-dimensional space that $T$ maps into itself. A complex operator on $N$ has an eigenvector, so $Tv = \lambda v$ for some $v \ne 0$.

steps.slogan: Contradict transitivity with the closed subspace $\ker(T - \lambda)$.
steps.detail:
The space $Y = \ker(T - \lambda)$ is closed, contains $v 
e 0$, and every $S' \in \mathcal{A}$ maps it into itself since $TS'w = S'Tw = \lambda S'w$. It is not $X$: a compact $\lambda I$ on an infinite-dimensional space forces $\lambda = 0$, but $T 
e 0$. So $\mathcal{A}v \subseteq Y 
e X$ is not dense, a contradiction.

concepts.c:compact-operator: Compactness supplies the compact set $K$ and the finite-dimensional eigenspace.
concepts.c:banach-space: Completeness is needed for Mazur's theorem and Schauder's theorem.
concepts.c:invariant-subspace: The theorem asks for a closed subspace that $T$ maps into itself.
concepts.c:eigenvector: An eigenvector of $T$ on a finite-dimensional space gives the contradicting subspace.
concepts.c:dense-set: Transitivity says that every nonzero orbit of the commutant is dense.
concepts.c:convex-hull: The image of $\Phi$ lies in a convex hull of compact sets, which is compact.

source.note: Lomonosov's theorem (Funct. Anal. Appl. 7 (1973), 213-214) in Hilden's short proof, as in Radjavi and Rosenthal, Invariant Subspaces; Aronszajn and Smith proved the compact case first (Ann. of Math. 60 (1954), 345-350).

statement: Let $X$ be a [simply connected space](c:simply-connected-space) and $k$ a field. The [Hochschild homology](c:hochschild-homology) of the cochain algebra $C^*(X;k)$ is isomorphic to the cohomology of the [free loop space](c:free-loop-space) $LX$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a [simply connected space](c:simply-connected-space).
The coefficients lie in a field $k$.

proofs.name: Eilenberg-Moore comparison
proofs.slogan: Present the free loop space as a homotopy pullback over $X \times X$, compare its cochains with a derived tensor product, and recognize the Hochschild complex.
proofs.scope: The outline treats spaces of finite type, where the Kunneth map is an equivalence; the cited paper builds the comparison through the cyclic bar construction. Only the isomorphism of graded vector spaces is claimed.

roles.why: Simple connectivity of $X$ and of $X \times X$ makes the Eilenberg-Moore spectral sequence converge.
Over a field the Kunneth and Eilenberg-Zilber maps identify the cochains of a product with a tensor product.

steps.slogan: Present the free loop space as a [homotopy pullback](c:homotopy-pullback) of the diagonal.
steps.detail: The [free loop space](c:free-loop-space) $LX$ is the homotopy pullback of the diagonal $\Delta\colon X \to X \times X$ along itself, through the path space fibration $X^I \to X \times X$.

steps.slogan: Apply the Eilenberg-Moore theorem to the pullback over $X \times X$.
steps.detail: Since $X \times X$ is [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space), the Eilenberg-Moore spectral sequence converges. It identifies $H^*(LX;k)$ with $\mathrm{Tor}_{C^*(X \times X)}(C^*(X), C^*(X))$, the cohomology of a derived tensor product of cochain modules.

steps.slogan: Replace the cochains of $X \times X$ by the tensor square of $C^*(X)$.
steps.detail: Over a field the Eilenberg-Zilber and Kunneth quasi-isomorphisms identify $C^*(X \times X)$ with $C^*(X) \otimes C^*(X)$ as algebras up to homotopy, compatibly with the module structures.

steps.slogan: Recognize the derived tensor product as the Hochschild complex.
steps.detail: The derived tensor product $C^*(X) \otimes^L_{C^*(X) \otimes C^*(X)} C^*(X)$ is computed by the bar resolution of $C^*(X)$ as a bimodule. That complex is the Hochschild complex of $C^*(X)$, the [cyclic bar construction](c:cyclic-bar-construction) of Jones.

steps.slogan: Take cohomology to get $H^*(LX;k) \cong HH_{-*}(C^*(X;k))$.
steps.detail: The cohomology of the Hochschild complex is $HH_*(C^*(X;k))$, and the quasi-isomorphism of step 4 matches it with the cochains of $LX$. The cohomological degree of $C^*$ is read as negative homological degree.

concepts.c:simply-connected-space: Simple connectivity makes the Eilenberg-Moore spectral sequence converge.
concepts.c:hochschild-homology: Hochschild homology of the cochain algebra is one side of the isomorphism.
concepts.c:free-loop-space: The cohomology of the free loop space is the other side of the isomorphism.
concepts.c:homotopy-pullback: The free loop space is a homotopy pullback of the diagonal.
concepts.c:cyclic-bar-construction: The cyclic bar construction is the Hochschild complex of the cochain algebra.

source.ref: J. D. S. Jones, Cyclic homology and equivariant homology, Inventiones Mathematicae 87 (1987), 403-423
source.note: The steps list the ingredients of the identification of Hochschild homology of cochains with loop space cohomology for simply connected spaces: the pullback square, Eilenberg-Moore convergence and the cyclic bar construction.

statement: Let a complex [reductive group](c:reductive-group) $G$ with maximal compact subgroup $K$ act algebraically on a finite-dimensional space $V$ with a $K$-invariant Hermitian norm. For $v \in V$ the orbit $Gv$ is closed if and only if the norm attains a minimum on $Gv$. Then the minimum points are the zeros of the [moment map](c:moment-map) on $Gv$ and form one $K$-orbit.

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a complex [reductive group](c:reductive-group) with a maximal compact subgroup $K$, acting algebraically on a finite-dimensional complex vector space $V$.
$V$ carries a Hermitian norm that is invariant under $K$.

conclusion: $Gv$ is closed exactly when $\|\cdot\|$ attains a minimum on $Gv$; the minimum points are the zeros of the moment map in $Gv$ and form a single $K$-orbit.

proofs.name: Convexity along the orbit
proofs.slogan: Show that the norm is convex along imaginary directions of the orbit, so critical points are minima and zeros of the moment map, then relate minima to closedness.
proofs.scope: The closed-orbit form of the theorem. The semistable version (the closure of an orbit meets the zero set of the moment map) and the Kirwan-Ness stratification are other members of the family and are not proved here.

roles.why: Reductivity gives the Cartan decomposition $G = K\exp(i\mathfrak{k})$ and the Hilbert-Mumford criterion for closed orbits.
A $K$-invariant norm makes the norm constant along $K$ and makes the moment map the derivative of the squared norm.

steps.slogan: Show that the squared norm is a convex function along the directions $\exp(it\xi)$.
steps.detail: Every element of $G$ is $k\exp(i\xi)$ with $k \in K$ and $\xi$ in the Lie algebra of $K$, and $\|kw\| = \|w\|$. In an eigenbasis of the Hermitian operator $i\xi$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_j$, $\|\exp(it\xi)v\|^2 = \sum_j e^{2t\lambda_j}|v_j|^2$, a [convex function](c:convex-function) of $t$.

steps.slogan: Identify the critical points of the norm on an orbit with the zeros of the moment map.
steps.detail: The derivative of $\|\exp(it\xi)v\|^2$ at $t = 0$ is $2\langle i\xi v, v\rangle$, which is the [moment map](c:moment-map) paired with $\xi$ up to normalization. So $v$ is critical on $Gv$ exactly when the moment map vanishes at $v$, and by convexity and $K$-invariance a critical point is a global minimum on $Gv$.

steps.slogan: Show that a closed orbit contains a vector of minimal norm.
steps.detail: The norm is a proper function on $V$, so it attains a minimum on a closed set such as $Gv$. By step 2 the minimizer is a zero of the moment map.

steps.slogan: Show that a vector of minimal norm has a closed orbit.
steps.detail: If $Gv$ were not closed, the Hilbert-Mumford criterion would give a one-parameter subgroup $\lambda$ with $\lim_{t \to 0}\lambda(t)v$ existing outside $Gv$. After a $K$-conjugation, which keeps the norm, $\lambda(e^s) = \exp(is\xi)$ and the convex function of step 1 is minimal at $s = 0$ and bounded as $s \to -\infty$, so it is constant there, which forces the limit to equal $v$, a contradiction.

steps.slogan: Show that the minimal vectors of one orbit form a single $K$-orbit.
steps.detail: Let $v$ and $gv$ be minimal with $g = k\exp(i\xi)$. The convex function $t \mapsto \|\exp(it\xi)v\|^2$ is minimal at $t = 0$ and $t = 1$, hence constant on $[0,1]$, which leaves only eigencomponents with $\lambda_j = 0$ and gives $\exp(i\xi)v = v$. So $gv = kv$.

steps.slogan: Assemble the equivalence, the moment map description and the single $K$-orbit.
steps.detail: Steps 3 and 4 give that $Gv$ is closed exactly when the norm has a minimum on $Gv$. Step 2 identifies the minimum points with the zeros of the moment map, and step 5 shows that they form one $K$-orbit.

concepts.c:reductive-group: Reductivity supplies the Cartan decomposition and the Hilbert-Mumford criterion.
concepts.c:moment-map: The moment map is the derivative of the squared norm along the orbit.
concepts.c:convex-function: Convexity turns critical points into global minima and gives uniqueness.

source.ref: G. Kempf and L. Ness, The length of vectors in representation spaces, in: Algebraic Geometry, Copenhagen 1978, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 732, Springer, 1979, 233-243
source.note: The steps list the ingredients of the Kempf-Ness argument: convexity of the norm along the orbit, critical points as zeros of the moment map, and closedness of orbits through the Hilbert-Mumford criterion.

statement: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of complete smooth [vector fields](c:vector-field) on a manifold $M$, $q_0 \in M$, $A$ the [attainable set](c:attainable-set) of $q_0$ (points $e^{t_k f_k} \cdots e^{t_1 f_1}(q_0)$ with $t_i \ge 0$, $f_i \in \mathcal{F}$) and $\mathcal{O}$ the orbit of $q_0$ (all real $t_i$). Then $A$ has nonempty interior in $\mathcal{O}$, and $A$ lies in the closure of that interior.

hypotheses.text: $\mathcal{F}$ is a family of complete smooth [vector fields](c:vector-field) on a smooth manifold $M$.
$q_0$ is a point of $M$, with [attainable set](c:attainable-set) $A$ and orbit $\mathcal{O}$ in the topology given by the orbit theorem.

proofs.name: Positive-time maps of maximal rank
proofs.slogan: Take a composition of positive-time flows of maximal rank, show that its image is open in the orbit, and repeat near each attainable point.
proofs.scope: The orbit form of Krener's theorem. When the Lie algebra rank condition holds at $q_0$, the orbit is open in $M$, so the interior is taken in $M$ itself.

roles.why: The fields supply the flows whose positive-time compositions fill out the attainable set and tangent spaces of the orbit.
The starting point $q_0$ fixes the orbit $\mathcal{O}$ and the attainable set $A$ that the theorem describes.

steps.slogan: Give the orbit $\mathcal{O}$ its manifold structure by the orbit theorem.
steps.detail: The Nagano-Sussmann orbit theorem makes $\mathcal{O}$ an immersed submanifold of $M$. Its tangent space at $q$ is spanned by the vectors $(P_* f)(q)$, where $P$ runs over compositions of flows of $\mathcal{F}$ and $f \in \mathcal{F}$.

steps.slogan: Choose a composition of positive-time flows of maximal rank.
steps.detail: For $q \in A$ consider the maps $t \mapsto e^{t_k f_k} \circ \cdots \circ e^{t_1 f_1}(q)$ on small positive times. Take one of maximal rank $r$ at some $t^*$; the image of a neighborhood of $t^*$ is an $r$-dimensional submanifold $N$ contained in $A$.

steps.slogan: Show that every field of $\mathcal{F}$ is tangent to $N$.
steps.detail: If some $f \in \mathcal{F}$ were transverse to $N$ at a point of $N$, adding the flow $e^{sf}$ with small $s > 0$ to the composition would raise the rank to $r + 1$. This contradicts maximality, so all fields of $\mathcal{F}$ are tangent to $N$.

steps.slogan: Deduce that $N$ is open in the orbit, so $A$ has interior.
steps.detail: Trajectories of fields tangent to $N$ stay in $N$, so $N$ is invariant under the local flows of $\mathcal{F}$. By the tangent space description of step 1, $\dim N = \dim \mathcal{O}$, so $N$ is open in $\mathcal{O}$ and $\operatorname{int}_{\mathcal{O}} A \ne \emptyset$.

steps.slogan: Repeat near any attainable point to put $A$ inside the closure of its interior.
steps.detail: Let $q_1 \in A$ and $W$ a neighborhood of $q_1$ in $\mathcal{O}$. Shortening the last flow time gives a point $q \in A \cap W$, and steps 2 to 4 with short times from $q$ give an open subset of $\mathcal{O}$ inside $A \cap W$. So every point of $A$ is a limit of interior points.

concepts.c:vector-field: The flows of the vector fields generate the attainable set and the orbit.
concepts.c:attainable-set: The attainable set is the set whose interior the theorem describes.

source.ref: A. A. Agrachev and Yu. L. Sachkov, Control Theory from the Geometric Viewpoint, Springer, 2004, chapter 8 (attainable sets); A. J. Krener, A generalization of Chow's theorem and the bang-bang theorem to nonlinear control problems, SIAM Journal on Control 12 (1974), 43-52
source.note: The steps list the ingredients of the published proof: the orbit theorem, maps of maximal rank on positive times, tangency of the fields and the repetition near attainable points.

statement: Let $f$ and $g$ be [analytic](c:analytic-function) near $x$, and let $v = x + y f(v)$ define $v$ near $x$ for small $|y|$. Then $g(v) = g(x) + \sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{y^k}{k!}\, \partial_x^{k-1}\big(f(x)^k g'(x)\big)$, and the [power series](c:power-series) in $y$ converges for small $|y|$.

hypotheses.text: The functions $f$ and $g$ are [analytic](c:analytic-function) in a neighborhood of the point $x$.
For small $|y|$ the value $v = v(x,y)$ solves $v = x + y f(v)$ with $v \to x$ as $y \to 0$.

proofs.name: Contour integral and integration by parts
proofs.slogan: Write each coefficient of $g(v)$ as a contour integral, change variable to $w = v - x$, integrate by parts and read the residue.
proofs.scope: The case $f(x) \ne 0$ in detail, and the case $f(x) = 0$ directly. This is the contour proof of the Lagrange-Burmann inversion formula, applied to $H(w) = g(x + w)$.

roles.why: Analyticity of $f$ and $g$ gives the implicit function, the inverse series and the contour integrals.
The equation $w = y\varphi(w)$ with $w \to 0$ selects the solution whose series is expanded.

steps.slogan: Solve the equation for $w = v - x$ as an analytic function of $y$.
steps.detail: Put $\varphi(w) = f(x + w)$, so $w = y\varphi(w)$. By the analytic implicit function theorem there is a unique small analytic solution $w(y)$ with $w(0) = 0$. If $f(x) = 0$ then $w \equiv 0$ and $g(v) = g(x)$, and the sum vanishes because $f^k g'$ has a zero of order at least $k$ at $x$; so assume $f(x) \ne 0$.

steps.slogan: Invert the relation $y = w/\varphi(w)$ near $w = 0$.
steps.detail: The function $\psi(w) = w/\varphi(w)$ is analytic near $0$ with $\psi(0) = 0$ and $\psi'(0) = 1/\varphi(0) \ne 0$. So $\psi$ is a local conformal bijection and $w(y)$ is its inverse.

steps.slogan: Write the coefficient of $y^k$ as a contour integral in the variable $w$.
steps.detail: Let $H(w) = g(x + w)$, so $g(v) = H(w(y))$. For $k \ge 1$ Cauchy's formula and the substitution $y = \psi(w)$ give $[y^k]\,H(w(y)) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint H(w)\,\frac{\psi'(w)\,dw}{\psi(w)^{k+1}} = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint H(w)\, d\!\left(-\frac{\psi(w)^{-k}}{k}\right)$ on a small circle around $0$.

steps.slogan: Integrate by parts around the closed contour.
steps.detail: The boundary term vanishes on a closed contour, so the integral becomes $\frac{1}{k}\cdot\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint H'(w)\,\psi(w)^{-k}\,dw$. Since $\psi^{-k} = \varphi^k / w^k$, this is $\frac{1}{k}\cdot\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint \frac{H'(w)\,\varphi(w)^k}{w^k}\,dw$.

steps.slogan: Read the residue as a derivative at $w = 0$ and sum over $k$.
steps.detail: The integral is the residue at $0$, namely $\frac{1}{(k-1)!}\,\partial_w^{k-1}\big(H'\varphi^k\big)(0)$. Because $H'(w) = g'(x+w)$ and $\varphi(w)^k = f(x+w)^k$, this equals $\partial_x^{k-1}\big(f^k g'\big)(x)/(k-1)!$. So the coefficient of $y^k$ is $\frac{1}{k!}\partial_x^{k-1}(f^k g')(x)$, and the $k = 0$ term is $g(x)$.

concepts.c:analytic-function: Analyticity gives the implicit function, power series and contour integrals.
concepts.c:power-series: The coefficients of the power series in $y$ are what the contour integral computes.

source.note: The classical contour-integral proof of the Lagrange-Burmann formula, as in Whittaker and Watson, A Course of Modern Analysis, chapter 7.

statement: Let $MU$ be the [complex cobordism](c:complex-cobordism) spectrum. Then $MU_*MU \cong MU_*[b_1, b_2, \dots]$ is a [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring) over $MU_*$ on generators $b_i$ of degree $2i$, and $(MU_*, MU_*MU)$ is a [Hopf algebroid](c:hopf-algebroid) that represents strict isomorphisms of [formal group laws](c:formal-group-law) over the [Lazard ring](c:lazard-ring) $MU_*$.
conclusion: $MU_*MU = MU_*[b_1, b_2, \dots]$, and its Hopf algebroid maps are those of the groupoid of formal group laws and strict isomorphisms.

proofs.name: Thom isomorphism and formal group laws
proofs.slogan: Identify $MU_*MU$ with $MU_*(BU)$ by the Thom isomorphism, compute it from the homology of $BU$, and match its structure maps with strict isomorphisms of formal group laws.
proofs.scope: The structure theorem for $MU_*MU$ as an outline of the cited proof. The Landweber-Novikov operations form the dual algebra, which is not treated here.

steps.slogan: Identify $MU \wedge MU$ with $MU \wedge BU_+$ by the Thom isomorphism.
steps.detail: Because $MU$ is complex oriented, the Thom isomorphism for the universal bundle gives an equivalence $MU \wedge MU \simeq MU \wedge BU_+$. Hence $MU_*MU \cong MU_*(BU)$ as $MU_*$-modules.

steps.slogan: Compute $MU_*(BU)$ from the integral homology of $BU$.
steps.detail: $H_*(BU;\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}[b_1, b_2, \dots]$ is polynomial and concentrated in even degrees. So the [Atiyah-Hirzebruch spectral sequence](c:atiyah-hirzebruch-spectral-sequence) collapses, and $MU_*(BU)$ is free over $MU_*$ on the monomials in the $b_i$, a [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring) $MU_*[b_1, b_2, \dots]$ under the product of $BU$.

steps.slogan: Identify $MU_*$ with the Lazard ring that classifies formal group laws.
steps.detail: Lazard's theorem says that the ring $L$ classifying one-dimensional formal group laws is polynomial on generators of degree $2i$, and Quillen's theorem identifies $MU_*$ with $L$. So the formal group law of $MU$ is universal.

steps.slogan: Read the two units as formal group laws joined by a strict isomorphism.
steps.detail: The left and right units $\eta_L, \eta_R\colon MU_* \to MU_*MU$ give two [formal group laws](c:formal-group-law) $F_L$ and $F_R$ over $MU_*MU$. The series $b(x) = \sum_{i \ge 0} b_i x^{i+1}$ with $b_0 = 1$ is a strict isomorphism between them, and it is universal: a ring map out of $MU_*MU$ is the same as a pair of formal group laws with a strict isomorphism.

steps.slogan: Match the Hopf algebroid maps with the groupoid of strict isomorphisms.
steps.detail: Composition of strict isomorphisms gives the coproduct, the identity isomorphism the counit and the inverse isomorphism the conjugation. The groupoid axioms are the Hopf algebroid axioms, so $(MU_*, MU_*MU)$ is a [Hopf algebroid](c:hopf-algebroid) with $MU_*MU = MU_*[b_1, b_2, \dots]$.

concepts.c:complex-cobordism: The spectrum $MU$ is the one whose self-homology the theorem computes.
concepts.c:polynomial-ring: The result says that $MU_*MU$ is a polynomial ring over $MU_*$.
concepts.c:hopf-algebroid: The pair of rings carries the structure maps that the theorem identifies.
concepts.c:formal-group-law: Strict isomorphisms of formal group laws are what $MU_*MU$ represents.
concepts.c:lazard-ring: The Lazard ring is the coefficient ring $MU_*$ over which $MU_*MU$ is polynomial.
concepts.c:atiyah-hirzebruch-spectral-sequence: It collapses for $BU$ because all cells are even.

source.ref: J. F. Adams, Stable Homotopy and Generalised Homology, University of Chicago Press, 1974, Part II; see also D. C. Ravenel, Complex Cobordism and Stable Homotopy Groups of Spheres, Academic Press, 1986, chapter 4
source.note: The steps list the ingredients of the structure theorem in Adams and Ravenel: the Thom isomorphism, the even-cell computation for BU, Lazard's theorem with Quillen's identification, and the groupoid of formal group laws; Landweber (1967) and Novikov (1967) found the structure first.

statement: Let $S = \{x + iy : x > 0,\ |y| < \pi/2\}$ and let $F$ be [continuous](c:continuous-function) on $\overline{S}$ and [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on $S$. If $|F| \le 1$ on $\partial S$ and $|F(z)| \le C\exp(A e^{c\,\mathrm{Re}\,z})$ for some $C, A > 0$ and $0 \le c < 1$, then $|F| \le 1$ on $S$.

hypotheses.text: $F$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) on the closed half-strip $\overline{S}$ and [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on $S$.
$|F| \le 1$ on the boundary $\partial S$.
$|F(z)| \le C\exp(A e^{c\,\mathrm{Re}\,z})$ on $S$ for constants $C, A > 0$ and $0 \le c < 1$.

proofs.name: Damping factor and maximum modulus
proofs.slogan: Multiply by a damping factor that beats the growth, apply the maximum modulus principle on long rectangles, then let the damping go to zero.
proofs.scope: The half-strip of width $\pi$; a half-strip of width $w$ reduces to it by an affine change of variable, with growth exponent below $\pi/w$. The statement about equal limits along the two edges is another member of the Lindelof family and is not proved here.

roles.why: Continuity up to the boundary and holomorphy inside allow the maximum modulus principle on rectangles.
The bound $1$ on the three finite sides of each rectangle starts the comparison.
The growth bound is slower than the damping factor, so the product decays at infinity.

steps.slogan: Multiply $F$ by the damping factor $E_\varepsilon(z) = \exp(-\varepsilon e^{c'z})$ with $c < c' < 1$.
steps.detail: Put $G_\varepsilon = F E_\varepsilon$. Since $|c'y| < c'\pi/2 < \pi/2$, we have $|E_\varepsilon(z)| = \exp(-\varepsilon e^{c'x}\cos(c'y)) \le 1$ on $\overline{S}$, and $\cos(c'y) \ge \kappa := \cos(c'\pi/2) > 0$. Hence $|G_\varepsilon| \le 1$ on $\partial S$.

steps.slogan: Show that $G_\varepsilon$ tends to zero as $x \to \infty$, uniformly in $y$.
steps.detail: We have $|G_\varepsilon(z)| \le C\exp(A e^{cx} - \varepsilon\kappa e^{c'x})$. Because $c < c'$, the exponent tends to $-\infty$ as $x \to \infty$, uniformly in $y$. So there is $R_0$ with $|G_\varepsilon| \le 1$ on $\{x \ge R_0\}$.

steps.slogan: Apply the [maximum modulus](c:maximum-modulus) principle on each rectangle $[0,R] \times [-\pi/2, \pi/2]$.
steps.detail: For $R \ge R_0$ the function $G_\varepsilon$ is continuous on the closed rectangle, holomorphic inside, and at most $1$ on its three sides in $\partial S$ and on the side $x = R$. So $|G_\varepsilon| \le 1$ on the rectangle, and since $R$ is arbitrary, on all of $\overline{S}$.

steps.slogan: Let $\varepsilon$ tend to zero to get $|F| \le 1$.
steps.detail: For fixed $z$, $E_\varepsilon(z) \to 1$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$. So $|F(z)| = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0}|G_\varepsilon(z)| \le 1$.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity up to the boundary lets the maximum modulus principle use boundary values.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy inside the half-strip makes the maximum modulus principle available.
concepts.c:maximum-modulus: The maximum modulus principle bounds $G_\varepsilon$ inside each rectangle by its boundary values.

source.note: The classical Phragmen-Lindelof damping argument (see Titchmarsh, The Theory of Functions, the section on the Phragmen-Lindelof theorem), written for the half-strip.
